item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports combining personal sequence modeling with population-level transition evidence. [TGCL4SR (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28789) combines a temporal item-transition graph with a time-aware sequence encoder. [GaGNN (2024)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S002002552400536X) fuses individual and group transition graphs to address sparse sequences. [MGUI (2026)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11506283) is especially relevant: recent-item gating, group-level sequence modeling, cross-user transition propagation, and user-specific mixture-of-experts fusion. These approaches model observed behavioral dependencies; they do not establish that transitions represent product compatibility or purchase completion.\n\nLearned routing also has precedent in [FamouSRec (WWW 2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3696410.3714663), which routes users among heterogeneous sequential encoders using frequency information. A practical adaptation—an implementation hypothesis, not a reported result—is SASRec plus a lightweight directed transition expert, with separate source/target embeddings and a gate conditioned on sequence state, history length, and transition support. Construct weighted edges exclusively from training histories; preserve direction and compare adjacent versus short-window transitions. Normalize or smooth counts to limit popularity dominance. Titles/descriptions could supply a separate TF-IDF or randomly initialized token-embedding expert trained on next-item prediction; semantic similarity should remain distinct from transition evidence. Evaluate sequence-only, graph-only, fixed fusion, and learned routing using the common macro validation HR@10. The cited work motivates these components but does not establish gains under this benchmark’s from-scratch constraints."}
